sections.title: E-1: Application
sections.summary: Establishes that Appendix E provides the procedures and criteria for design and construction of roller-compacted concrete (RCC) pavement (RCCP), and states that RCCP use on airfield pavements is prohibited unless specifically approved.
sections.body: Appendix E provides the procedures and criteria applicable to the design and construction of roller-compacted concrete (RCC) pavement (RCCP). RCCP is prohibited for airfield pavement use unless approved by the USACE Transportation Systems Center (TSC) or the appropriate Tri-Service Pavement Discipline Working Group (TSPDWG) Service representative.
key_points: Appendix E covers design and construction procedures/criteria for RCC pavement (RCCP).
RCCP use on airfield pavements is prohibited unless approved by the USACE TSC or the appropriate TSPDWG Service representative.
sections.applicability: Applies to all DoD RCC pavement projects; governs whether RCCP may be used, particularly the airfield-use restriction.

sections.title: E-2: General
sections.summary: Defines RCC pavement as a no-slump PCC mixture placed and compacted using asphalt-paving-like techniques with no forms, dowels, or reinforcing steel, describes its 10-30%+ cost savings versus formed/slipformed concrete, notes its rougher surface limits it to low-speed heavy-load traffic, and lists non-pavement applications.
sections.body: RCCP is a concrete paving process that involves laydown and compaction of a no-slump PCC mixture using techniques similar to hot-mix asphalt (HMA) paving. RCC combines existing HMA paving and cement-treated base construction procedures with the final product of a PCC pavement. This construction technique can place a large amount of concrete quickly with no forms, dowels, or reinforcing steel. Construction cost savings of 10 to 30 percent, or even more, compared to slipformed or fixed-formed concrete pavements have been realized. The surface smoothness and texture of RCC pavement is somewhat rougher and coarser than conventional concrete pavement, which tends to limit RCC pavement applications to areas where low-speed, heavy-load traffic is the primary user. Non-pavement applications using a similar construction method include slope protection of embankments or dams, impermeable linings for sludge drying basins or wastewater lagoons, platforms for handling containerized freight, and surfaces for recycling yards, composting yards, log sorting yards, and mine storage areas.
key_points: RCCP is a no-slump PCC mixture placed and compacted using techniques similar to HMA paving (laydown + roller compaction), with no forms, dowels, or reinforcing steel.
Combines HMA paving and cement-treated base construction procedures to produce a PCC pavement product quickly and inexpensively.
Reported construction cost savings of 10 to 30 percent or more compared to slipformed or fixed-formed concrete pavement.
Surface is rougher/coarser than conventional PCC, limiting use mainly to low-speed, heavy-load traffic areas.

Non-pavement uses include slope protection of embankments/dams, impermeable linings for sludge/wastewater lagoons, and platforms/yards for freight, recycling, composting, log sorting, and mine storage.
sections.applicability: Provides background for deciding whether RCCP is an appropriate paving method for a given low-speed, heavy-load-traffic pavement or a similar non-pavement application.

sections.title: E-3: Construction Process
sections.summary: Overview of the RCCP construction sequence: continuous pugmill mixing, base preparation, paver placement, compaction (vibratory then pneumatic-tired rollers), 7-14 day moist curing, and the definition/classification of cold joints (perpendicular, longitudinal, transverse) and contraction joint sawcutting practice.
sections.body: RCC is typically mixed in a continuously mixing pugmill plant located near the paving site, where aggregates, cement, and fly ash are weighed with belt scales or volumetrically proportioned on a continuous conveyor belt and dumped into the pugmill, where water is added and vigorously mixed. The freshly mixed RCC is discharged into covered dump trucks for hauling. At the paving site, the base course is graded, compacted, and moistened just before RCC placement, with stringlines set to guide paving screed height. The RCC is placed with a paving machine to uniform density and smoothness, then immediately compacted with several passes of a dual-drum vibratory roller to specified final densities, followed by several passes of a rubber-tired roller to tighten surface texture, with optional finish rolling by steel-drum rollers to remove roller marks. After rubber-tire rolling, the surface is kept moist with fogger-spray water trucks until an irrigation sprinkler system is set up, keeping the RCC continuously moist for the curing period, usually 7 days (14 days is better); membrane-forming curing compounds and asphalt emulsions are also successful. Cold joints are construction joints formed between paving lanes placed more than one hour apart, and always between two separate days of paving; they are classified as perpendicular (between lanes placed perpendicular to each other), longitudinal (oriented in the direction of paving), or transverse (perpendicular to the direction of paving, between lanes oriented the same direction). Transverse cold joints are constructed by sawing across the rounded-off ends of paving lanes and removing excess material. Transverse contraction joints may be sawcut 4 to 20 hours after RCC placement and compaction; while RCC pavement has historically been allowed to crack naturally, current practice favors sawcutting contraction joints to improve pavement aesthetics and ease sealant application/maintenance.
key_points: RCC is mixed in a continuous pugmill plant (belt-scale or volumetric proportioning) and hauled to the paving site in covered dump trucks.
Base course is graded, compacted, and moistened before RCC placement; stringlines guide paving screed height.
Compaction sequence: dual-drum vibratory roller passes to target density, then rubber-tired roller passes to tighten surface texture, with optional steel-drum finish rolling to remove roller marks.
Curing keeps the surface continuously moist (fogger spray, then sprinkler irrigation) typically for 7 days (14 days is better); membrane curing compounds and asphalt emulsions are also effective.
Cold joints form between paving lanes placed more than 1 hour apart or on different days; classified as perpendicular, longitudinal, or transverse.
Transverse cold joints are formed by sawing across the rounded lane ends and removing excess material; transverse contraction (sawcut) joints may be cut 4-20 hours after placement/compaction.
Current practice favors sawcutting contraction joints (vs. historically allowing natural cracking) to improve aesthetics and ease sealant application/maintenance.
sections.applicability: Describes the general RCCP construction sequence from mixing through curing and joint formation, applicable to all DoD RCCP projects.

sections.title: E-4: Subgrade and Base Course Preparation
sections.summary: Requires the subgrade and base course to conform to UFC 3-250-01/UFC 3-260-02, notes RCC freeze-thaw durability is not fully understood despite generally satisfactory field performance, and calls for adequate base drainage in frost areas and sufficient base support for full RCCP consolidation.
sections.body: The subgrade and base course should conform to the requirements outlined in UFC 3-250-01 and UFC 3-260-02. The freeze-thaw durability of RCC is not fully understood, but the long-term performance of non-air-entrained RCCP is generally satisfactory, despite marginal laboratory performance. For this reason, in areas where the pavement or base course might be subject to seasonal frost action, particular attention should be given to providing a base course that adequately drains any water infiltrating through the pavement or subgrade. The base course should also provide sufficient support to permit full consolidation of the RCCP through its entire thickness upon compaction.
key_points: Subgrade/base course requirements follow UFC 3-250-01 and UFC 3-260-02.
RCC freeze-thaw durability is not fully understood, but field performance of non-air-entrained RCCP has generally been satisfactory despite marginal laboratory performance.
In seasonal frost areas, the base course must adequately drain water infiltrating through the pavement/subgrade.
Base course must provide sufficient support to allow full consolidation of the RCCP through its entire thickness during compaction.
sections.applicability: Applies when designing the subgrade/base course to support RCCP construction, especially in frost-susceptible areas.

sections.title: E-5: Selection of Materials
sections.summary: Framing section for RCC material-selection subsections: general aggregate-source considerations plus specific requirements for coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, other/nonconventional aggregates, cement, and admixtures used in RCC mixtures.
sections.body: This section introduces the material-selection topics for RCC pavement, covered in the following subsections: E-5.1 General considerations for aggregate source selection, E-5.2 Coarse Aggregate, E-5.3 Fine Aggregate, E-5.4 Other Aggregates (nonconventional sources such as asphalt/base-course aggregate), E-5.5 Cement, and E-5.6 Admixtures.
key_points: Introduces material-selection subsections: general aggregate selection, coarse aggregate, fine aggregate, other aggregates, cement, and admixtures.
Aggregate source selection is described as one of the most important factors in RCC quality and economy.
sections.applicability: Framing section for RCC material selection topics covered in E-5.1 through E-5.6.

sections.title: E-5.1: General
sections.summary: States that aggregate source selection is one of the most important factors in RCC quality/economy, presents Table E-1's recommended combined RCC gradation (asphalt-concrete-like, intended to minimize surface voids), and notes the well-graded blend may be hard to produce from only two aggregate groups.
sections.body: One of the most important factors in determining the quality and economy of concrete is the selection of a suitable aggregate source. The recommended RCC gradation is shown in Table E-1. This gradation is similar to gradations used for asphalt concrete and should produce an RCCP surface with relatively few surface voids. Conventional PCC mixtures are generally obtained by combining coarse and fine aggregates; however, the well-graded blend of aggregates given in Table E-1 may be difficult to produce from only two aggregate groups due to segregation of the different-sized particles. When possible, using more than two aggregate groups (coarse and fine) at the plant provides more flexibility in blending aggregates to control the gradation of the RCC. Table E-1 (Recommended Combined RCC Gradation) gives cumulative percent passing, by weight, for eleven sieve sizes from 25 mm (1 in.) down to 0.075 mm (No. 200): 25 mm (1 in.) = 100 percent passing; 19 mm (3/4 in.) = 85-100 percent; 12.5 mm (1/2 in.) = 70-95 percent; 9.5 mm (3/8 in.) = 55-85 percent; 4.75 mm (No. 4) = 40-65 percent; 2.36 mm (No. 8) = 30-55 percent; 1.18 mm (No. 16) = 20-45 percent; 0.60 mm (No. 30) = 15-35 percent; 0.30 mm (No. 50) = 10-25 percent; 0.15 mm (No. 100) = 5-15 percent; and 0.075 mm (No. 200) = 2-10 percent.
key_points: Table E-1 recommended combined RCC gradation (cumulative % passing by weight): 25 mm (1 in.) = 100; 19 mm (3/4 in.) = 85-100; 12.5 mm (1/2 in.) = 70-95; 9.5 mm (3/8 in.) = 55-85; 4.75 mm (No. 4) = 40-65; 2.36 mm (No. 8) = 30-55.
This combined gradation resembles asphalt concrete gradations and is intended to minimize surface voids in the finished RCCP.
The well-graded blend may be difficult to produce from only two aggregate groups (coarse+fine) due to segregation; using more than two stockpile groups gives more blending flexibility.
tables: Table E-1: Recommended Combined RCC Gradation
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and blending aggregates to meet the recommended RCC gradation for pavement-quality RCCP.

sections.title: E-5.2: Coarse Aggregate
sections.summary: Covers acceptable coarse aggregate sources (crushed/uncrushed gravel, recycled concrete, crushed stone), ASTM C33 quality guidance, the need for consistent grading throughout production, and the nominal maximum aggregate size limit (the source text states 19 mm as both 0.25 in. and 0.75 in. in adjacent sentences).
sections.body: The coarse aggregate may consist of crushed or uncrushed gravel, recycled concrete, crushed stone, or a combination thereof. The quality of coarse aggregate used by the Corps of Engineers to date in RCCP generally complies with ASTM C33, although satisfactory RCC is possible with coarse aggregate not meeting these requirements; local state highway department coarse aggregate grading limits, for example, are generally acceptable. Regardless of the grading limits imposed, the grading of aggregate delivered to a project must be relatively consistent throughout the production of RCC, an important factor in maintaining control of the mixture's workability. The nominal maximum aggregate size normally should not exceed 19 mm (given in the source text as 0.25 in.), particularly if pavement surface texture is a consideration; using aggregate larger than 19 mm (given in the source text as 0.75 in.) results in segregation, and rock pockets are likely.
key_points: Coarse aggregate may be crushed/uncrushed gravel, recycled concrete, crushed stone, or a combination; Corps quality generally follows ASTM C33 though non-conforming aggregate can still work.
Grading must remain relatively consistent throughout production to control mixture workability, regardless of which grading limits are used.

Nominal maximum aggregate size normally should not exceed 19 mm, particularly where surface texture matters (the source text gives inconsistent inch equivalents of 0.25 in. and 0.75 in. for the same 19 mm value in adjacent sentences).
Aggregate larger than 19 mm causes segregation and rock pockets.
sections.applicability: Applies when specifying/selecting coarse aggregate source, gradation, and maximum size for RCC mixtures.

sections.title: E-5.3: Fine Aggregate
sections.summary: Covers fine aggregate sourcing (natural/manufactured sand), ASTM C33-based quality with a relaxed No. 200 fines limit (up to 8% in Canada), benefits/risks of nonplastic silt vs. clay fines, ASTM C128 Note 3 testing for high-fines sands, and the tradeoffs of using minimally processed pit-/quarry-run aggregate.
sections.body: Fine aggregate may consist of natural sand, manufactured sand, or a combination of the two, and should be composed of hard, durable particles. Fine aggregate quality is based on the limits given in ASTM C33, except consideration should be given to relaxing the maximum 5.0 percent limit of material finer than the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve; Canada has increased the amount of material passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve to 8 percent of total aggregate weight with acceptable results. Sands with higher quantities of nonplastic silt particles may be beneficial as mineral filler and may allow some reduction in the amount of cement required; however, mixtures made with fine aggregates having an excessive amount of clay may have a high water demand, with attendant shrinkage, cracking, and reduced strength. The specific gravity and absorption of sands with high quantities of fines should be determined according to Note 3 in ASTM C128. Expedient construction with RCC can utilize minimally processed aggregates, such as pit- or quarry-run aggregates, to produce an RCC pavement, though this RCC pavement may require greater water content, be less durable, and have a lower flexural strength.
key_points: Fine aggregate may be natural sand, manufactured sand, or a blend, composed of hard, durable particles; quality generally based on ASTM C33 limits.
The ASTM C33 maximum of 5.0% material finer than the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve may be relaxed; Canada has used up to 8% with acceptable results.
Nonplastic silt fines can act as beneficial mineral filler and may allow reduced cement content; excessive clay fines increase water demand, shrinkage, and cracking, and reduce strength.
Specific gravity and absorption for sands with high fines content should be determined per Note 3 of ASTM C128.
Expedient construction may use minimally processed pit- or quarry-run aggregate, but the resulting RCCP may need more water, be less durable, and have lower flexural strength.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting and qualifying fine aggregate sources for RCC mixtures, including fines-content decisions.

sections.title: E-5.4: Other Aggregates
sections.summary: Notes that aggregate produced for asphalt paving and base courses has performed successfully as RCC aggregate, typically producing a tighter surface texture due to higher fines content but requiring more attention to stockpiling/handling due to segregation risk across its wide size range.
sections.body: Recent experience with RCC shows that aggregate produced for uses other than PCC is successful as aggregate for RCC; material produced for asphalt paving and base courses is effective as RCC aggregate. These materials typically have a higher percentage of fines passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve than conventional concrete aggregates and, as a result, may produce a "tighter" pavement surface texture. Because these aggregates range in size from 19 mm (0.75 in.) to the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve, control of the grading may be more difficult due to segregation; therefore, due attention should be directed toward stockpile formation and subsequent handling of a single-size-group aggregate.
key_points: Aggregate produced for asphalt paving or base courses has performed successfully as RCC aggregate.
These aggregates typically have more fines passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve than conventional concrete aggregate, producing a tighter pavement surface texture.
Because these aggregates span a wide size range (19 mm to 0.075 mm), grading control is more difficult due to segregation, requiring careful stockpile formation and handling.
sections.applicability: Applies when considering nonconventional (asphalt/base-course) aggregate sources for RCC mixtures.

sections.title: E-5.5: Cement
sections.summary: Requires Portland cement used in RCC to meet ASTM C595, Type I or II.
sections.body: The Portland cement for use in RCC must meet the requirements of ASTM C595, Type I or II. This single ASTM C595 blended-hydraulic-cement requirement is the only cement-quality specification given for RCC pavement mixtures in this appendix; the full CRD-C 203/ASTM C595 citation appears in Appendix G.
key_points: Portland cement for RCC must meet ASTM C595, Type I or II.
This is the only cement-quality specification given for RCC mixtures in Appendix E; the corresponding CRD-C 203/ASTM C595 citation is listed in Appendix G.
sections.applicability: Applies to cement specification/selection for RCC pavement mixtures.

sections.title: E-5.6: Admixtures
sections.summary: Explains that a proper air-void system prevents frost damage but has limited field trials in RCC; describes low w/cm ratio plus high compaction as the primary strategy to minimize freeze-thaw damage, and discusses limited effectiveness and cost-justification requirements for water-reducing/retarding admixtures.
sections.body: A proper air void system prevents frost damage in concrete that freezes when critically saturated. Research indicates that air-entrained RCC pavement mixtures can be successfully produced in the laboratory; however, field production and placement have only been tried on a very limited basis. The most widely used method to minimize freezing and thawing damage to RCC pavement is to combine a low w/cm ratio with a highly compacted RCC; the low w/cm ratio and good compaction ensure the concrete has a minimum amount of freezable water in the capillaries and has low permeability, making it difficult for sufficient water to enter the RCC and reach critical saturation. A free-draining base under the RCC pavement will further prevent water from saturating the RCC pavement; as long as the RCC pavement is not critically saturated, freezing and thawing will cause no damage. Laboratory studies show that water-reducing or -retarding admixtures are successful with RCC but not as effective as in conventional concrete because they affect the paste content of the mixture, and RCC contains less paste than conventional PCC mixtures. If these admixtures are proposed, their use should be based on investigations demonstrating that the benefits outweigh the cost.
key_points: A proper air-void system prevents frost damage in critically saturated concrete; air-entrained RCC has succeeded in the lab but has only limited field trials.
The primary strategy to minimize freeze-thaw damage is a low w/cm ratio combined with high compaction, minimizing freezable water and permeability so the RCC does not reach critical saturation.
A free-draining base course further helps prevent RCC saturation; if not critically saturated, freeze-thaw causes no damage.

Water-reducing/retarding admixtures work with RCC but are less effective than in conventional concrete because RCC has less paste content; their use should be justified by investigation showing benefit exceeds cost.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating air entrainment or chemical admixtures for RCC frost resistance and workability.

sections.title: E-6: Mixture Proportioning
sections.summary: Framing section for RCC mixture-proportioning subsections: general proportioning considerations plus three specific proportioning methods (CRD-C 161, ASTM D558, ACI 207.5R).
sections.body: This section introduces RCC mixture-proportioning topics, covered in the following subsections: E-6.1 General proportioning considerations and how RCC differs from conventional concrete, E-6.2 the CRD-C 161 Method (currently recommended), E-6.3 the ASTM D558 Method, and E-6.4 the ACI 207.5R Method.
key_points: Introduces general RCC mixture-proportioning considerations and three specific methods: CRD-C 161, ASTM D558, and ACI 207.5R.
sections.applicability: Framing section for RCC mixture proportioning subsections E-6.1 through E-6.4.

sections.title: E-6.1: General
sections.summary: Explains that RCC cannot simply be produced by reproportioning conventional concrete via a single change, lists the 4 key property differences (no air entrainment, lower water/paste content, higher fine aggregate content), names 5 available proportioning methods, and identifies CRD-C 161 as currently recommended.
sections.body: The basic mixture proportioning procedures and properties of conventional concrete and RCC are essentially the same; however, conventional concrete cannot be reproportioned for use as RCC by any single action such as (1) altering proportions of the mortar and concrete aggregates, (2) reducing the water content, (3) changing the w/cm ratio, or (4) increasing the fine aggregate content. Differences in mixture proportioning procedures and properties are mainly due to the relatively dry consistency of the fresh RCC and the selected use of nonconventionally graded aggregates. The primary differences in the properties of RCC are (1) RCC generally is not air entrained, (2) RCC has a lower water content, (3) RCC has a lower paste content, and (4) RCC generally requires a higher fine aggregate content to limit segregation. Several methods are available to proportion RCC pavement mixtures, including those found in CRD-C 161, ASTM D558, EM 1110-2-2006, ACI 211.3, and ACI 207.5R. The first two of these methods treat the material as cement-stabilized soil rather than concrete and establish a relationship between moisture and the density obtained from a particular compactive effort; the latter three methods follow an approach similar to that used in proportioning conventional concrete. Currently, CRD-C 161 is the method recommended for RCC pavement mix design. The procedures for RCC pavement mixture proportioning are not as well defined as for conventional concrete; the key to successfully selecting an RCC trial batch that performs well in the field is the experience of the laboratory personnel conducting the proportioning study.
key_points: Conventional PCC cannot simply be reproportioned into RCC by altering mortar/aggregate ratio, reducing water, changing w/cm, or raising fine-aggregate content alone.
RCC differs from conventional concrete in 4 ways: generally not air-entrained, lower water content, lower paste content, and higher fine-aggregate content needed to limit segregation.
Five proportioning methods are available: CRD-C 161, ASTM D558, EM 1110-2-2006, ACI 211.3, and ACI 207.5R.
CRD-C 161 and ASTM D558 treat RCC as a cement-stabilized soil (moisture-density relationship); EM 1110-2-2006, ACI 211.3, and ACI 207.5R follow a conventional-concrete-like proportioning approach.
CRD-C 161 is currently the recommended method for RCC pavement mix design.
Success in selecting a trial batch depends heavily on the experience of the laboratory personnel conducting the proportioning study.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting a mixture-proportioning method and understanding the fundamental differences between RCC and conventional PCC mix design.

sections.title: E-6.2: CRD-C 161 Method
sections.summary: Describes CRD-C 161 as covering proportioning of RCC mixtures with 19 mm nominal maximum aggregate for vibratory-screed paver placement, based on test data/experience or first-approximation estimates, verified by trial batches.
sections.body: This method covers the procedures for proportioning RCC mixtures with 19 mm (0.75 in.) nominal maximum size aggregates and having a workability suitable for placement with the vibratory screed of an asphalt paving machine. Select RCCP mixture proportions based on test data or experience with the materials actually used. Where such data or experience is limited or not available, estimates given in this standard practice provide a first approximation for air-entrained or non-air-entrained RCCP mixture proportions. Check these proportions by trial batches in the laboratory or field and adjust as necessary to achieve the desired RCC characteristics.
key_points: CRD-C 161 covers proportioning for RCC mixtures with 19 mm nominal maximum aggregate suited to vibratory-screed paver placement.

Proportions should be based on test data or experience with the actual materials; where unavailable, the standard provides first-approximation estimates for air-entrained or non-air-entrained mixtures.
Proportions must be verified via laboratory or field trial batches and adjusted as needed to achieve desired RCC characteristics.
sections.applicability: Applies as the currently recommended mixture-proportioning method for RCC pavement mix design.

sections.title: E-6.3: ASTM D558 Method
sections.summary: Describes ASTM D558-based proportioning as determining optimum moisture content for maximum density, and notes that the related CRD-C 653 optimum moisture may produce a mixture too wet for efficient vibratory roller operation.
sections.body: A proportioning based on ASTM D558 has produced satisfactory RCC mixtures. The method produces the optimum moisture content necessary to obtain maximum density for a particular set of materials and compaction procedures. Previous tests indicate that the optimum moisture content obtained by CRD-C 653 may produce a mixture too wet to allow efficient operation of a vibratory roller.
key_points: ASTM D558-based proportioning determines the optimum moisture content for maximum density under a given compaction procedure.
Prior testing indicates the CRD-C 653 optimum moisture content may produce a mixture too wet for efficient vibratory roller operation.
sections.applicability: Applies as an alternative moisture-density-based mixture-proportioning method for RCC.

sections.title: E-6.4: ACI 207.5R Method
sections.summary: Describes the ACI 207.5R method's central selection of the paste-to-mortar volume ratio Pv, its effect on compactability and surface texture, the satisfactory Pv range of 0.36-0.41, and inclusion of sub-No.200 fine aggregate fines in the Vp calculation.
sections.body: The method in ACI 207.5R, with some modifications, is used on many RCC mixtures. The primary consideration for this method is proper selection of the ratio (Pv) of the air-free volume of paste (Vp) to the air-free volume of mortar (Vm). This selection is based primarily upon the grading and particle shape of the fine aggregate. The Pv affects both the compactability of the mixture and the resulting surface texture of the pavement. Ratios of 0.36 to 0.41 are satisfactory for mixtures having a nominal maximum size aggregate of 19 or 38 mm (0.75 or 1.5 in.). The fraction of fine aggregate finer than the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve should be included in Vp when calculations use Pv.
key_points: ACI 207.5R method centers on the paste-to-mortar volume ratio Pv = Vp/Vm, selected mainly from fine-aggregate grading and particle shape.
Pv affects both mixture compactability and resulting pavement surface texture.
Pv ratios of 0.36 to 0.41 are satisfactory for mixtures with 19 mm or 38 mm (0.75 or 1.5 in.) nominal maximum aggregate size.
The fraction of fine aggregate passing the 0.075 mm (No. 200) sieve is included in Vp when computing Pv.
sections.applicability: Applies as a conventional-concrete-style proportioning method for RCC based on the paste/mortar volume ratio.

sections.title: E-7: Mixture Properties
sections.summary: Framing section for RCC mixture-properties subsections: handling/workability characteristics, laboratory sample fabrication, and strength test results.
sections.body: This section introduces RCC mixture-properties topics, covered in the following subsections: E-7.1 Handling Characteristics (workability), E-7.2 Sample Fabrication (laboratory cylinder/beam specimens), and E-7.3 Strength Results.
key_points: Introduces RCC handling characteristics, sample fabrication, and strength results subsections.
sections.applicability: Framing section for RCC mixture-properties subsections E-7.1 through E-7.3.

sections.title: E-7.1: Handling Characteristics
sections.summary: Explains that RCC workability is judged via soil-compaction optimum-moisture concepts (since slump testing is not meaningful for a no-slump mixture), notes field optimum water content typically runs 0.1-0.5% above lab-determined optimum, and requires a test section per project.
sections.body: The workability of RCC determines its capacity for successful mixing, placement, and compaction; it embodies the concepts of compatibility and, to some degree, moldability and cohesiveness. The same factors that affect the workability of conventional concrete affect RCC: the grading, particle shape, and proportion of the aggregate; the cementitious material content; and the presence of chemical and mineral admixtures. However, the effect of each factor is not necessarily of the same magnitude for RCC as for conventional concrete. The slump test measures the consistency of conventional concrete but is not meaningful for RCC since it has no slump. A preliminary judgment of the workability, placeability, and compactibility of RCC pavement mixtures is made during mixture proportioning studies by determining the optimum moisture content using soil compaction concepts, per the soil compaction procedures described in CRD-C 161, paragraphs 7.1 through 7.6. Experience indicates that the actual optimum RCC water content necessary in the field may need to be slightly greater than the lab-determined optimum moisture content, probably due to loss of water from evaporation during transport and placement or to different compaction in the field; ambient conditions determine the water content variation, with typical moisture increases of 0.1 to 0.5 percent above optimum. A test section is constructed for each RCC project to adjust the mixture proportions as necessary to achieve the required workability.
key_points: RCC workability is judged using soil-compaction concepts (optimum moisture content per CRD-C 161 paragraphs 7.1-7.6) since the conventional slump test is not meaningful for a no-slump mixture.
Actual field optimum water content is typically 0.1 to 0.5 percent above the lab-determined optimum, due to evaporation during transport/placement and differing field compaction.
A test section is constructed for each RCC project to adjust mixture proportions as needed to achieve required workability.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating and adjusting RCC workability during mixture-proportioning studies and field construction.

sections.title: E-7.2: Sample Fabrication
sections.summary: States w/cm ratio and compaction control RCC strength (Corps mixtures to date used w/cm 0.30-0.40), describes cylindrical specimen fabrication per ASTM C1176/CRD-C 160, and details the CRD-C 161 two-layer beam-molding procedure with vibration and surcharge.
sections.body: Primarily, the w/cm ratio and the degree of compaction attained control the strength of an RCC mixture. All RCC pavement mixtures placed by the Corps of Engineers to date had w/cm ratios ranging from 0.30 to 0.40. Cylindrical laboratory test specimens for strength determinations are fabricated per ASTM C1176 or CRD-C 160. There is no standardized procedure for fabricating RCC beam specimens to determine concrete flexural strength; however, as described in CRD-C 161, some success has been achieved by filling beam molds in two layers, consolidating by vibrating each layer on a vibrating table having a frequency of 3,600 vibrations per minute under a surcharge of 57 kg (125 lb), uniformly distributing the surcharge over the entire specimen area during molding, and vibrating until a ring of mortar forms around the complete periphery of the mold. All specimens fabricated in the laboratory are cured according to ASTM C192.
key_points: w/cm ratio and degree of compaction primarily control RCC strength; Corps RCCP mixtures to date used w/cm ratios of 0.30 to 0.40.
Cylindrical specimens are fabricated per ASTM C1176 or CRD-C 160.

No standardized beam-fabrication procedure exists; CRD-C 161 describes filling beam molds in two layers, each vibrated on a table at 3,600 vibrations/min under a 57 kg (125 lb) surcharge until a mortar ring forms around the periphery.
All laboratory-fabricated specimens are cured per ASTM C192.
sections.applicability: Applies when fabricating laboratory RCC test specimens (cylinders or beams) for mixture proportioning or strength verification.

sections.title: E-7.3: Strength Results
sections.summary: Explains that lab-fabricated/cured specimens generally show higher strength than field cores/sawn beams due to higher achieved unit weight (98-99% of theoretical maximum vs. 95-98% for cores) and more efficient moist curing, and recommends fabricating a low-density companion specimen set during proportioning studies.
sections.body: Test specimens fabricated and cured in the laboratory generally exhibit higher strengths than those cored or sawn from an RCCP. This is probably due to the higher unit weights typically obtained with the fabricated specimens and the more efficient laboratory moist curing. Laboratory test specimens generally have unit weights that are 98 to 99 percent of the theoretical maximum (air-free) weight of the mixture, while core samples taken from RCCP typically have unit weights ranging from 95 to 98 percent of the theoretical weight. Therefore, during the laboratory mixture proportioning studies, consideration should be given to fabricating a companion set of test specimens having the lowest relative density allowed by the contract specifications.
key_points: Laboratory-fabricated/cured specimens generally show higher strength than field cores/sawn beams, due to higher achieved unit weight and more efficient moist curing.
Lab specimens typically reach 98-99% of theoretical maximum (air-free) density; field cores typically reach only 95-98%.
During proportioning studies, fabricate a companion set of specimens at the lowest relative density permitted by the contract specifications.
sections.applicability: Applies when interpreting laboratory vs. field strength results and setting proportioning-study specimen density targets.

sections.title: E-8: Thickness Design
sections.summary: Framing section for RCC thickness-design subsections: general basis/no-load-transfer assumption, lift thickness limits, and two-lift construction.
sections.body: This section introduces RCC thickness-design topics, covered in the following subsections: E-8.1 General (design basis and the no-load-transfer assumption), E-8.2 Lift Thickness, and E-8.3 Two-Lift Construction.
key_points: Introduces thickness-design subsections: general basis, lift thickness limits, and two-lift construction.
sections.applicability: Framing section for RCC thickness-design subsections E-8.1 through E-8.3.

sections.title: E-8.1: General
sections.summary: States that RCC thickness design follows UFC 3-250-01/UFC 3-260-02 assuming NO joint/crack load transfer (vs. measured 16-19% at contraction cracks, still below the 25% used for plain concrete), covers structure-adjacent construction practice, and notes tested flexural strengths run 20-50% above design assumptions though conventional design remains standard.
sections.body: The thickness design procedure for RCC pavement is outlined in UFC 3-250-01 and UFC 3-260-02. The primary difference in the approaches to RCC pavement and plain concrete pavement thickness design is the assumption of no load transfer at any joint or crack in the RCC pavement. Limited load transfer tests conducted at Fort Hood, Texas and Fort Stewart, Georgia revealed average load transfer at transverse contraction cracks of 16 to 19 percent; load transfer at longitudinal and construction joints will be lower, and all values were less than the 25 percent used for plain concrete pavement design for parking areas, open storage areas, and airfields. Placement of RCC pavement immediately adjacent to existing structures is not practical; conventional formed concrete should be used between the structure and the RCC pavement, with the RCC pavement placed first and cut back to the desired line, or placed against the previously placed formed concrete. Beams sawn from various RCCP at various locations have shown that the actual flexural strength of the pavement was 20 to 50 percent higher than the typical strength assumed in the design for those pavements, suggesting that thickness design for compacted RCCP could be modified based upon the 28-day strength of beams sawn from a test section constructed using the same aggregate, cement, and construction procedure planned for the entire work; however, until additional performance records and testing procedures are developed for RCCP, conventional pavement thickness design will be used.
key_points: Thickness design procedure follows UFC 3-250-01 and UFC 3-260-02; the key difference from plain concrete design is assuming NO load transfer at any RCCP joint or crack.

Field load-transfer tests (Fort Hood, Fort Stewart) measured 16-19% average load transfer at transverse contraction cracks, all below the 25% used for plain concrete design of parking/storage areas/airfields.
RCC should not be placed directly against existing structures; use conventional formed concrete as a transition (RCC placed first and cut back, or placed against pre-existing formed concrete).
Sawn beams from constructed RCCP have shown actual flexural strength 20-50% higher than typical design assumptions, but conventional thickness design remains standard pending more performance data.
sections.applicability: Applies to the general basis and no-load-transfer assumption underlying RCC pavement thickness design.

sections.title: E-8.2: Lift Thickness
sections.summary: Gives the paver-governed maximum uncompacted lift thickness (250-300 mm/10-12 in.), the 1.25x rule-of-thumb for estimating uncompacted from design thickness, and the 100 mm (4 in.) minimum lift thickness.
sections.body: The maximum thickness of a lift of RCCP is governed by the ability of the pavers to place the RCCP in a smooth and continuous fashion. This maximum uncompacted thickness is usually 250 to 300 mm (10 to 12 in.). The maximum uncompacted thickness can be approximated by multiplying the design thickness by 1.25, thus accounting for the reduction in thickness due to compaction. The minimum thickness of any lift should be 100 mm (4 in.).
key_points: Maximum uncompacted lift thickness is governed by paver capability, typically 250-300 mm (10-12 in.).
Approximate uncompacted thickness = design (compacted) thickness x 1.25, to account for compaction-induced thickness reduction.
Minimum lift thickness should be 100 mm (4 in.).
sections.applicability: Applies when determining single-lift RCCP placement thickness limits.

sections.title: E-8.3: Two-Lift Construction
sections.summary: Covers when/why two or more lifts are used, the monolithic-vs-rigid-overlay design choice depending on the 1-hour fresh-joint bonding window, the 2/3 first-lift thickness rule, and the multi-lift trigger when total thickness exceeds twice the paver's maximum lift capacity.
sections.body: If the total uncompacted thickness exceeds the capacity of the paver, the RCCP should be placed in two or more lifts, thus creating a horizontal joint (or horizontal plane between the layers) in the RCCP. Sufficient bond develops at a fresh horizontal joint in RCCP (top lift placed within one hour of bottom lift) to allow the use of a monolithic thickness design; if the top lift is not placed within one hour of the bottom lift, the thickness should be designed as a rigid overlay of a rigid base pavement. The surface of the lower lift should be kept moist and clean until the upper lift is placed, and the upper lift should be placed and compacted within one hour of compacting the lower lift to ensure a bond between lifts is formed. In two-lift construction, the uncompacted thickness of the first lift should be two-thirds the total uncompacted height of the RCCP (or the maximum lift thickness the paver can handle, whichever is smaller); the thinner section in the upper lift aids in creating a smoother final surface and, because of the smaller volume of material, allows the paver placing the second lift to move quicker than and follow closer behind the paver placing the first lift. Multiple lifts will be necessary if the total uncompacted thickness of the RCCP is greater than twice the maximum lift capacity of the paver.
key_points: Two-lift (or more) construction is used when total uncompacted RCCP thickness exceeds paver capacity, creating a horizontal joint between lifts.
A monolithic thickness design may be used if the top lift is placed within 1 hour of the bottom lift (fresh horizontal joint bond); otherwise design as a rigid overlay on a rigid base pavement.
First (bottom) lift uncompacted thickness = two-thirds of total uncompacted height (or the paver's max lift capacity, whichever is smaller).
Upper lift must be placed and compacted within 1 hour of compacting the lower lift to ensure bond.
Multiple lifts are required if total uncompacted RCCP thickness exceeds twice the paver's maximum lift capacity.
sections.applicability: Applies when RCCP total uncompacted thickness exceeds a single paver lift's capacity.

sections.title: E-9: Test Section
sections.summary: Framing section for RCC test-section subsections: general requirements, optimum rolling passes determination, nuclear gauge/lab correlation calibration block, and strength tests.
sections.body: This section introduces the RCCP test-section requirements, covered in the following subsections: E-9.1 General, E-9.2 Optimum Number of Rolling Passes, E-9.3 Nuclear Density Gauge/Lab Density Correlation Calibration Block, and E-9.4 Strength Tests.
key_points: Introduces test section subsections: general requirements, optimum rolling passes, gauge calibration block, and strength tests.
sections.applicability: Framing section for RCC test-section subsections E-9.1 through E-9.4.

sections.title: E-9.1: General
sections.summary: Requires a test section built with production materials/equipment at least 10 days before production paving, sized to establish rolling patterns and density correlations, containing all joint types, with a suggested minimum layout of two 3.7-4.3 m wide, 38 m long lanes.
sections.body: A test section must be constructed to determine the ability of the contractor to mix, haul, place, compact, and cure RCC pavement. The test section must be constructed of the same material using the same equipment intended to be used in production placement, at a location near the jobsite at least 10 days before construction of the RCC pavement. The test section should be large enough to establish the rolling pattern for the vibratory and finish rollers, the correlation between laboratory and nuclear gauge densities, and the correlation between the number of passes and relative density. The density tests should be obtained with a nuclear gauge in accordance with ASTM C1040. The test section should contain both longitudinal and transverse cold joints and a fresh joint. A suggested minimum size is two 3.7- to 4.3-m (12 to 14 ft)-wide lanes, with each joint type a minimum of 38 m (125 ft) long, with one and one-half lanes placed the first day and the rest placed the next day.
key_points: A test section is required at least 10 days before production paving, built with the same materials/equipment as production, to verify contractor mixing/hauling/placing/compacting/curing ability.
Test section must be large enough to establish the roller pattern, lab-to-nuclear-gauge density correlation, and passes-vs-relative-density correlation; density measured per ASTM C1040.
Must include longitudinal cold joints, transverse cold joints, and a fresh joint.
Suggested minimum size: two 3.7-4.3 m (12-14 ft) wide lanes, each joint type at least 38 m (125 ft) long, with 1.5 lanes placed the first day and the remainder the next day.
sections.applicability: Applies to planning and constructing the required RCCP test section before production paving begins.

sections.title: E-9.2: Optimum Number of Rolling Passes
sections.summary: Describes using a same-hole nuclear gauge (direct transmission, calibration-block-standardized) after each vibratory pass until readings change less than 1% to set the minimum passes for target density, with a hard 4-pass minimum.
sections.body: During the test strip construction, use a nuclear gauge operated in the direct transmission mode and standardized with a calibration block to determine the optimum number of passes with the vibratory roller to reach maximum density. The density should be measured by inserting the nuclear gauge probe into the same hole after each pass of the vibratory roller; the hole should be made with an instrument specifically designed for the purpose, formed using the same method throughout the test section and main construction. This rolling and measuring procedure should be continued until there is less than a 1 percent change in successive readings. These data may be used in conjunction with correlation between the nuclear gauge and the laboratory density to determine the minimum number of passes needed to achieve or slightly exceed the specified density in the RCCP construction; however, a minimum of four vibratory passes should be used, and this minimum will probably prevail in most cases.
key_points: The nuclear gauge (direct transmission mode) measures density after each vibratory roller pass, using the same probe hole, until successive readings change by less than 1%.
This determines the minimum number of passes needed to achieve or slightly exceed the specified density.
A minimum of 4 vibratory passes is always required, and will likely govern in most cases.
sections.applicability: Applies when determining the optimum/minimum number of vibratory roller passes during test section construction.

sections.title: E-9.3: Nuclear Density Gauge/Lab Density Correlation Calibration Block
sections.summary: Details the daily calibration block procedure: RCC-mixture block sized 460x460 mm by lift-thickness-plus-25mm, compacted to 98-100% of ASTM D1557 max wet density, used to derive a daily correction factor from three averaged full-depth gauge readings, with two gauges calibrated for redundancy.
sections.body: Use a calibration block each day before paving begins to calibrate the full-depth readings of the nuclear density gauges. The block should be fabricated from the RCC mixture to be used in the project before the test section construction begins. The block size should be 460 mm by 460 mm (18 in. by 18 in.) by the maximum thickness of one lift, plus 25 mm (1 in.). The block should be compacted to between 98 and 100 percent of the maximum wet density determined in accordance with ASTM D1557. The block should be measured and weighed to determine the actual density (unit weight) and used to check the calibration of the nuclear density gauge. After drilling a hole in the block to accommodate the nuclear density gauge probe, three full-depth nuclear density gauge tests should be performed in the direct transmission mode and the results averaged; this average nuclear density gauge reading should then be compared with the measured unit weight of the block, and the difference used as a correction factor for all readings taken that day. If the adjusted nuclear gauge density is less than the specified density, additional passes with the vibratory roller should be made on the fresh RCC until the specified density is reached. Two nuclear density gauges should be calibrated (using the same holes) during the test section construction, so that an extra one is available during construction.
key_points: A calibration block is fabricated from the project's RCC mixture, sized 460 x 460 mm (18 x 18 in.) by max lift thickness plus 25 mm (1 in.), compacted to 98-100% of ASTM D1557 max wet density.
Three full-depth nuclear gauge readings in a drilled probe hole are averaged and compared to the block's measured (weighed) unit weight to derive a daily correction factor.
Two nuclear density gauges are calibrated using the same holes during test section construction so a spare is available during production.
sections.applicability: Applies to the daily nuclear gauge calibration procedure using a project-specific RCC calibration block.

sections.title: E-9.4: Strength Tests
sections.summary: Requires flexural and splitting tensile strength testing of test-section samples, with mix/compaction/curing adjustment and a rebuilt test section if design strength is not met.
sections.body: Pavement strength is determined from samples obtained from the test section. The testing should determine the flexural and splitting tensile strength of the RCC pavement. If the design strength requirements are not met, adjust the mix proportions (or alter the compaction procedure or curing, and build another test section) until the strength results meet specifications.
key_points: Test section samples are tested for flexural and splitting tensile strength to verify pavement design strength.
If strength requirements are not met, adjust mix proportions, compaction procedure, or curing, and build another test section until specifications are satisfied.
sections.applicability: Applies to verifying RCCP design strength via test-section sampling before production paving.

sections.title: E-10: Batching, Mixing, and Transporting
sections.summary: Covers RCC mixing plant selection (twin-shaft pugmill; continuous vs. batch-type plants), minimum plant capacity for larger jobs, and hauling requirements including a 15-minute maximum haul time and covered dump trucks.
sections.body: RCC requires a vigorous mixing action to disperse the relatively small amount of water evenly throughout the matrix; this action has been best achieved by using a twin shaft pugmill mixer as commonly used in asphalt concrete mixing. RCC may be produced successfully in either a continuous mixing plant or batch-type plant. The continuous mixing plant is recommended for mixing RCC because it is easier to transport to the site, takes less time to set up, and has a greater output (or production) capacity than the batch-type plant; the batch-type plant allows more accurate control over the proportions of material in each batch but generally does not have enough output capacity for larger paving jobs. The most widely used and recommended equipment is a continuous plant with weight controls (belt scales) for the materials. The output of the plant should be such that the smooth, continuous operation of the paver(s) is not interrupted. Generally, for all but the smaller jobs (840 m2 [1,000 yd2] or smaller), the capacity of the plant should be no less than 225 metric tons (250 tons) per hour, matching the laydown capacity of the paver(s) and rollers. The plant should be located as close as possible to the paving site, but in no case should the haul time between the batch plant and the paver(s) exceed 15 minutes. The RCC should be hauled from the mixer to the paver(s) in dump trucks equipped with protective covers to guard against adverse environmental effects such as rain or extreme cold or heat; the truck should dump the concrete directly into the paver hopper.
key_points: A twin-shaft pugmill mixer (as used in asphalt concrete mixing) provides the vigorous mixing needed to disperse RCC's relatively small water content.
Continuous mixing plants are recommended over batch-type plants for RCC: easier to transport/set up and higher output, though batch plants control proportions more precisely.
For jobs larger than 840 m2 (1,000 yd2), plant capacity should be at least 225 metric tons (250 tons) per hour, matching paver/roller laydown capacity.
Haul time between the batch plant and paver(s) should never exceed 15 minutes; RCC is hauled in covered dump trucks that dump directly into the paver hopper.
sections.applicability: Applies to selecting and operating the RCC batching/mixing plant and transport logistics for a paving project.

sections.title: E-11: Placing
sections.summary: Covers paving machine requirements (automatic grade control, tamping bars), feed/screw adjustments for RCC's stiff volume, the 45-minute placement/compaction time limit and 60-minute adjacent-lane limit for a fresh joint, and echelon paving to reduce cold joints.
sections.body: For most pavement applications, RCC should be placed with a paving machine. The paver should be equipped with automatic grade control devices such as a traveling ski or electronic stringline grade control device, and pavers should have at least two tamping bars; these machines provide a satisfactory surface texture and some initial compaction when the RCC is placed. Necessary adjustments on the paver to handle the RCC include enlarging the feeding gates between the feed hopper and the screed to accommodate the large volume of stiff material moving through the paver, and adjusting the spreading screws in front of the screed to ensure the RCC is spread uniformly across the width of the paving lane. Care should be taken to keep the paver hopper from becoming empty to prevent any gaps or other discontinuities from forming in the pavement. The concrete should be placed and compacted within 45 minutes after water has been added to the batch. When paving adjacent lanes, the new concrete should be placed within 60 minutes of placing the first lane to form a fresh joint; this time may have to be reduced depending on ambient conditions, and if these time restraints cannot be met, a cold joint is formed. The height of the screed should be set even with the uncompacted height of the adjacent lane, allowing simultaneous compaction of the edges of the adjacent lanes into a fresh joint. Two or more pavers operating in echelon may reduce the number of cold joints by one-half or greater, and are especially recommended in road construction where the entire width of the road can be placed at the same time.
key_points: RCC is placed with a paving machine with automatic grade control (traveling ski or electronic stringline) and at least 2 tamping bars.
Feed gates should be enlarged and spreading screws adjusted to handle the large volume of stiff RCC material uniformly.
RCC must be placed and compacted within 45 minutes of water addition; adjacent lanes must be placed within 60 minutes of the first lane to form a fresh (not cold) joint.
Two or more pavers operating in echelon can cut the number of cold joints by half or more, especially valuable for road construction.
sections.applicability: Applies to paver setup, operation, and timing requirements during RCC placement.

sections.title: E-12: Compaction
sections.summary: Framing section for RCC compaction subsections: general equipment/passes, proper rolling timing, rolling pattern, lane-end compaction, proper roller operation, and finish rolling.
sections.body: This section introduces RCC compaction procedures, covered in the following subsections: E-12.1 General, E-12.2 Proper Time for Rolling, E-12.3 Rolling Pattern, E-12.4 Compacting the End of a Lane, E-12.5 Proper Roller Operation, and E-12.6 Finish Rolling.
key_points: Introduces compaction subsections: general equipment, timing, rolling pattern, lane-end compaction, roller operation, and finish rolling.
sections.applicability: Framing section for RCC compaction subsections E-12.1 through E-12.6.

sections.title: E-12.1: General
sections.summary: Describes the standard dual-drum 9-metric-ton vibratory roller (4+ passes) plus optional 18-metric-ton pneumatic-tired roller finishing, dual-drum static roller mark removal, and the single-drum vibratory roller alternative.
sections.body: RCCP has usually been compacted with a dual-drum (9 metric ton [10 ton] static weight) vibratory roller making four or more passes over the surface to achieve the design density (one back-and-forth motion is two passes). To achieve a higher quality pavement, the primary compaction should be followed with two or more passes of an 18 metric ton (20 ton) pneumatic-tired roller (620 kPa [90 psi] minimum tire pressure) to close up any surface voids or cracks. The use of a dual-drum static (non-vibratory) roller may be required to remove any roller marks left by the vibratory or pneumatic-tired roller. A single-drum (9 metric ton [10 ton]) vibratory roller has been successfully used to compact RCCP but may require the use of a pneumatic-tired or dual-drum static roller to remove tire marks.
key_points: RCCP is usually compacted with a dual-drum (9 metric ton/10 ton static weight) vibratory roller making 4 or more passes (1 back-and-forth = 2 passes).
For higher quality, follow with 2+ passes of an 18 metric ton (20 ton) pneumatic-tired roller at 620 kPa (90 psi) minimum tire pressure to close surface voids/cracks.
A dual-drum static roller may be needed afterward to remove roller marks; a single-drum vibratory roller has also been used successfully, with pneumatic-tired or static rolling to remove tire marks.
sections.applicability: Applies to the general equipment train and pass counts for compacting RCC pavement.

sections.title: E-12.2: Proper Time for Rolling
sections.summary: Sets the 10-minute placement-to-rolling limit and 45-minute overall rolling completion window, and describes reading mixture consistency (too wet = rubbery/deep ruts, too dry = poor consolidation) from the initial static passes.
sections.body: The consistency of the RCC when placed should be such that it may be compacted immediately behind the paver without undue displacement of the RCC pavement surface; if rolling has to be delayed, the cause should be investigated and the problem corrected. In no case should more than 10 minutes pass between placement and the beginning of the rolling procedure. The rolling should be completed within 45 minutes of the time the water was added at the mixing plant. A good indication that the RCC is ready for compaction is obtained by observing the displacement of the surface after two static passes with the 9 metric ton (10 ton) vibratory roller. A mixture that is too wet may appear "rubbery" under the roller, or even spread to form a deep rut after two passes; a mixture that is too dry will hardly consolidate at all under the first passes. In either case, only minor changes in the design water content should be made at the plant to correct the problem; otherwise, a new mix design may be needed. With practice, the roller operator should be able to tell whether the consistency of the RCC is satisfactory for compaction.
key_points: Rolling must begin within 10 minutes of placement and be completed within 45 minutes of water addition at the mixing plant.

Readiness for compaction is judged by observing surface displacement after 2 static passes of the 9 metric ton (10 ton) vibratory roller: "rubbery" behavior or deep rutting indicates too wet, minimal consolidation indicates too dry.
Only minor water-content adjustments at the plant should be needed to correct consistency problems; otherwise a new mix design may be required.
sections.applicability: Applies to timing and readiness judgment for beginning RCC compaction after placement.

sections.title: E-12.3: Rolling Pattern
sections.summary: Details the standard 4-pass vibratory pattern for both the first lane (exterior edge, then interior edge left uncompacted for the fresh joint) and adjacent lanes, and how the pattern differs for a cold-joint interior edge.
sections.body: After making the static passes, the vibratory roller should make four vibratory passes on the RCCP using the following pattern: two passes on the exterior edge of the first paving lane (the perimeter of the parking area or the edge of a road) so that the rolling wheel extends over the edge of the pavement 25 to 50 mm (1 to 2 in.) (done to "confine" the RCCP to help prevent excessive lateral displacement of the lane upon further rolling), followed by two passes within 300 to 450 mm (12 to 18 in.) of the interior edge. This will leave an uncompacted edge to set the height of the screed for an adjacent lane and allows both lanes of the fresh joint to be compacted simultaneously. Any remaining uncompacted material in the center of the lane should be compacted with two passes of the roller, and this pattern should be repeated once to make a total of four passes on the lane (or more if the specified density is not achieved). If the interior edge will be used to form a cold joint, it should be rolled exactly as the exterior edge was rolled, taking care to maintain a level surface at the joint and not round the edge. When the adjacent lane is placed, two passes should be made about 300 to 450 mm (12 to 18 in.) from the outer edge of the lane (again, to confine the concrete), followed by two passes on the fresh joint; the first two passes should extend 25 to 50 mm (1 to 2 in.) over the outer edge of this adjacent lane if the lane will form an outer edge of the completed pavement. Any remaining uncompacted material in the lane should be rolled with two passes of the roller, and this pattern should be repeated to make a total of four passes over the RCCP. Additional passes may be necessary along the fresh joint to ensure smoothness and density across the joint.
key_points: Standard 4-pass vibratory rolling pattern: 2 passes on the exterior lane edge (wheel overhanging 25-50 mm/1-2 in. to confine the lane), then 2 passes within 300-450 mm (12-18 in.) of the interior edge, leaving the interior edge uncompacted to set adjacent-lane screed height.

The uncompacted interior edge allows simultaneous compaction of both lanes at a fresh joint; if it instead forms a cold joint, it is rolled the same as the exterior edge, keeping the surface level (not rounded).

Remaining center material is compacted with 2 additional passes, repeating the exterior/interior pattern to reach 4 total passes (more if density is not achieved); additional passes may be needed along the fresh joint for smoothness/density.
sections.applicability: Applies to the standard vibratory roller pattern for compacting RCC paving lanes and fresh/cold joints.

sections.title: E-12.4: Compacting the End of a Lane
sections.summary: Describes the rounded-ramp problem at lane ends and the two acceptable fixes: full-depth power sawing to a vertical face (preferred) or half-depth sawing plus hand trimming.
sections.body: When the end of a lane is reached, the roller should roll off the end of the lane, creating a rounded ramp. The recommended procedure is to cut the ramp with a power saw full depth to form a vertical face; this will eliminate hand work and lessen the possibility of damage to the in-place RCC pavement. Another method is to saw the concrete to at least one-half the depth of the pavement, then trim the lower portion of the joint by hand to form a nearly vertical face, clean of debris and loose particles.
key_points: At the end of a paving lane, the roller creates a rounded ramp that should be cut full-depth with a power saw to form a vertical face (preferred, avoids hand work/damage risk).
Alternative: saw to at least half the pavement depth, then hand-trim the remainder to a nearly vertical, clean face.
sections.applicability: Applies to finishing/joint preparation at the terminal end of an RCC paving lane.

sections.title: E-12.5: Proper Roller Operation
sections.summary: Covers vibrator on/off timing rules relative to roller motion, staggering stop points to avoid depressions, and the general high-amplitude/low-frequency (or low-amplitude/high-frequency) speed guidance.
sections.body: During vibratory compaction, the roller should never stop on the pavement with the vibrator on; instead, the vibrator should be turned on only after the roller is in motion and should be turned off several feet before the roller stops moving. The stopping points of successive rolling passes should be staggered to avoid forming depressions in the fresh pavement surface. The roller should be operated at the proper speed, amplitude, and frequency to achieve optimum compaction; experience has shown that the best compaction will probably occur at high amplitude and low frequency (because of the thick lifts) and a speed not exceeding 2 km (1.5 mi.) per hour. A low amplitude/high frequency combination may be necessary if the surface is disturbed during the high amplitude rolling.
key_points: The vibrator must never run while the roller is stationary; turn it on only after the roller is moving and off several feet before stopping.
Stagger the stopping points of successive passes to avoid forming depressions in the fresh surface.
Best compaction generally occurs at high amplitude/low frequency and a speed not exceeding 2 km/hr (1.5 mph); switch to low amplitude/high frequency if the surface is disturbed at high amplitude.
sections.applicability: Applies to correct vibratory roller operating technique during RCC compaction.

sections.title: E-12.6: Finish Rolling
sections.summary: Describes finish rolling with pneumatic-tired roller passes to close surface voids, optional light dual-drum passes to remove marks, and the requirement to keep exposed surfaces moist until curing begins.
sections.body: The vibratory compaction should be immediately followed with two or more passes of the pneumatic-tired roller so the surface voids and fissures close to form a tight surface texture. This rolling may be followed by a light dual-drum roller to remove any roller marks on the surface, but this will probably not be necessary. It is very important that all exposed surfaces of the RCCP be kept moist with a light water spray after the rolling process until the curing procedure is implemented.
key_points: Vibratory compaction is immediately followed by 2+ pneumatic-tired roller passes to close surface voids/fissures and achieve a tight surface texture.
A light dual-drum roller pass may follow to remove roller marks, though this is usually unnecessary.
Exposed RCCP surfaces must be kept moist with a light water spray after rolling until curing begins.
sections.applicability: Applies to the final rolling steps that establish RCCP surface texture before curing.

sections.title: E-13: Cold Joints
sections.summary: Framing section for RCC cold-joint subsections: general definition/timing, construction procedure, contraction-joint sawing, joint/crack sealing, load-transfer devices, and two-lift vertical joint alignment.
sections.body: This section introduces RCC cold joint topics, covered in the following subsections: E-13.1 General, E-13.2 Cold Joint Construction, E-13.3 Sawing of Contraction Joints, E-13.4 Sealing Joints and Cracks, E-13.5 Load-Transfer Devices, and E-13.6 Vertical Joints in Two-Lift Construction.
key_points: Introduces cold joint subsections: general, construction, sawing of contraction joints, sealing, load-transfer devices, and two-lift vertical alignment.
sections.applicability: Framing section for RCC cold joint subsections E-13.1 through E-13.6.

sections.title: E-13.1: General
sections.summary: Defines a cold joint as forming when the first RCC lane has hardened (typically after about 1 hour) too much to consolidate with the fresher second lane, most often occurring at the end of a day's paving.
sections.body: A cold joint in RCC pavement is somewhat analogous to a construction joint in conventional concrete pavement. It is formed between two adjacent lanes of RCC when the first lane has hardened to such an extent that the uncompacted edge cannot be consolidated with the fresher second lane. This happens when there is some time delay between placement of adjacent lanes, such as at the end of the day's construction; this hardening typically takes approximately one hour, depending on properties of the concrete and environmental conditions. The adjacent lane should be placed against the first lane and compacted within this time frame; otherwise, the joint between the two lanes should be considered a cold joint.
key_points: A cold joint forms between adjacent RCC lanes when the first lane has hardened too much (typically after about 1 hour) to consolidate with the fresher second lane.
Analogous to a construction joint in conventional concrete pavement; commonly occurs at the end of a day's paving.
sections.applicability: Applies to identifying when a lane-to-lane joint becomes a cold joint requiring special construction treatment.

sections.title: E-13.2: Cold Joint Construction
sections.summary: Details longitudinal and transverse cold-joint construction: sawing/trimming the hardened edge to a vertical face, dampening it, overlapping screed height, pushing back excess material without broadcasting, and rolling technique to achieve a smooth joint.
sections.body: Before placing fresh concrete against hardened in-place pavement to form a longitudinal cold joint, the edge of the in-place pavement should be cut with a power concrete saw. The recommended procedure is to saw full depth with a power concrete saw to form a vertical face, eliminating hand work and lessening the possibility of damage to the in-place pavement; another method is to saw to at least one-half the depth of the pavement, then trim the lower unsawed portion of the joint by hand to form a nearly vertical face, clean of debris and loose particles, taking care to avoid undercutting the pavement edge. This vertical face should be dampened before the placement of the fresh lane begins. The height of the screed should be set to a sufficient elevation to compensate for the reduction in thickness due to compaction, overlapping the edge of the hardened concrete surface 25 to 75 mm (1 to 3 in.). The excess fresh concrete should be pushed back to the edge of the fresh concrete with rakes or lutes and rounded off so no fresh material is left on the surface of the hardened concrete before compacting the joint; the loose material should not be broadcast over the area to be compacted, as this may leave a rough surface texture after rolling. The edge of the fresh lane adjacent to the hardened concrete should be rolled first in the static mode, with about 300 mm (1 ft) of the roller on the fresh concrete, to form a smooth longitudinal joint. Transverse cold joints are constructed in a similar manner: after cutting back the rounded-off edge and wetting the vertical face, the paver is backed into place and the screed set to the proper elevation using shims sitting on top of the hardened concrete; excess material is pushed back, and a static pass is made in the transverse direction across the first 300 mm (1 ft) of the freshly placed lane, with the joint carefully rolled to ensure a smooth surface transition.
key_points: Before placing fresh RCC against hardened pavement, saw the edge full depth (preferred) or at least half depth plus hand-trimming, to form a clean, nearly vertical face; dampen the face before placing fresh concrete.

Screed height is set to overlap the hardened edge 25-75 mm (1-3 in.), compensating for compaction thickness loss; excess fresh material is pushed back and rounded off, never broadcast over the compaction area.

The fresh lane edge adjacent to hardened concrete is rolled first in static mode (about 300 mm/1 ft of roller on fresh concrete) to form a smooth joint; transverse cold joints are constructed similarly using shims to set screed elevation.
sections.applicability: Applies to forming both longitudinal and transverse cold joints in RCC pavement construction.

sections.title: E-13.3: Sawing of Contraction Joints
sections.summary: Explains the shift from allowing natural cracking to sawcutting contraction joints, gives the 1/4-depth sawing requirement with a 3 mm blade, notes green-cut saws and the critical 4-20 hour sawing window, and gives the 9-18 m typical spacing with a 12 m no-backup-data ceiling.
sections.body: RCC pavement has been allowed to crack naturally in many previous projects to save the cost of sawing joints; however, this has probably resulted in larger crack openings, increased raveling, and higher maintenance costs than if cracking was controlled. Contraction joints may be sawn in RCC pavement to induce controlled crack formation; the weakened plane should be sawn at least one-fourth the slab depth using a 3 mm (1/8 in.) blade. Sawing of joints can commence when the concrete strength is sufficient to enable the saw to cut through the concrete with a minimum of spalling, tearing, or aggregate pullouts. The use of special green-cut saws that penetrate the pavement surface to only a depth of about 1 in. have been shown to be effective on at least one RCC paving project. The time of sawing is very important and usually ranges from 4 to 20 hours after compaction, depending on weather conditions and other factors. To date, sawn transverse contraction joints in RCC pavement have typically been spaced from 9 to 18 m (30 to 60 ft); these spacings may vary with different materials and thicker pavements, so optimum contraction joint spacing should be determined during test section construction, and local service records may also be helpful. Joint spacing greater than 12 m (40 ft) should never be used without backup data.
key_points: Sawn contraction joints (weakened plane sawn to at least 1/4 slab depth with a 3 mm/1/8 in. blade) are now favored over allowing RCC to crack naturally, which caused larger crack openings and higher maintenance.
Sawing timing is critical, typically 4 to 20 hours after compaction depending on weather; special green-cut saws penetrating only about 1 in. have been effective on at least one project.
Typical sawn transverse contraction joint spacing is 9-18 m (30-60 ft); spacing greater than 12 m (40 ft) should never be used without supporting data.
sections.applicability: Applies to determining whether/how to sawcut contraction joints and their spacing in RCC pavement.

sections.title: E-13.4: Sealing Joints and Cracks
sections.summary: Explains why inadequate joint/crack seal maintenance causes rapid rigid-pavement deterioration through incompressible-material intrusion, restricted movement, spalling/cracking, slab breakage, and subgrade fines migration/loss of edge support.
sections.body: Rigid pavements that do not receive adequate joint and crack seal maintenance will rapidly deteriorate due to the intrusion of water and incompressible materials that migrate through and into the pavement joints and cracks. Incompressible materials lodge between the individual pavement slabs and parts of slabs, restricting movement that allows for expansion and contraction; this restriction of movement causes spalling and cracking along the edges of the joints and cracks and can result in breakage and blowup of entire slabs. Water in the subgrade material causes a migration of fines that eventually results in loss of support under the edge of the pavement slab.
key_points: Without adequate joint/crack seal maintenance, rigid pavements deteriorate rapidly from water and incompressible-material intrusion.
Incompressible material restricts joint movement, causing spalling, cracking, and potential slab breakage/blowup.
Water reaching the subgrade migrates fines, eventually causing loss of support beneath slab edges.
sections.applicability: Applies to the rationale for and consequences of joint/crack sealing (or its absence) in RCC pavement maintenance.

sections.title: E-13.5: Load-Transfer Devices
sections.summary: Notes that RCCP's stiff consistency makes conventional dowels/keyed joints impractical to install, so dowel use should be limited until an efficient insertion/alignment method is developed.
sections.body: The stiff consistency of RCCP does not lend itself to application of load-transfer devices such as dowels or keyed joints. Until an efficient method is developed to insert and align dowels properly in RCCP, the use of dowels should be limited.
key_points: RCCP's stiff consistency makes conventional load-transfer devices (dowels, keyed joints) impractical to install.
Dowel use should be limited until an efficient method for properly inserting and aligning dowels in RCCP is developed.
sections.applicability: Applies to decisions about load-transfer device use at RCCP joints.

sections.title: E-13.6: Vertical Joints in Two-Lift Construction
sections.summary: Requires aligning cold transverse and longitudinal joints between the upper and lower lifts into a single uniform vertical face, cutting back the lower lift if the edges are not aligned.
sections.body: In two-lift construction, care should be taken to align the cold transverse and longitudinal joints in the upper and lower lifts to form a uniform, vertical face through the depth of the pavement along the joint. If the edge of the upper lift is not even with the edge of the lower lift, the lower lift should be cut back even with the edge of the upper lift.
key_points: In two-lift construction, cold joints in the upper and lower lifts must be aligned to form a single uniform vertical face through the pavement depth.
If the lifts' edges are not aligned, the lower lift is cut back to match the upper lift's edge.
sections.applicability: Applies to joint alignment between lifts in two-lift RCC pavement construction.

sections.title: E-14: Curing
sections.summary: Framing section for RCC curing subsections: general moist-curing practice, effect of moist curing on frost resistance, and early loading restrictions.
